narrative: A Palestinian refugee and long-term resident of the Yarmouk neighborhood of Damascus had been carrying out medical work in the besieged camp. He was wanted by all sides: by the Syrian regime, whose forces had already shot and injured him twice; by armed opposition groups, because he had stayed in Yarmouk after Jabhat al-Nusra and Daesh took control of most of it; and by Islamist groups, because of his leftist political beliefs and lack of religious observance. One night in December 2015 he was told he must be ready to leave the next morning and to bring no documents. An arrangement had been made with a member of the government's security forces to get him out of Yarmouk for about 300,000 Syrian pounds, roughly US$1,400, per person. He prepared in total secrecy, because if Jabhat al-Nusra heard someone was leaving they would detain and torture them. At the first checkpoint, held by the Free Syrian Army, he crossed by pretending to be Egyptian. At the next, controlled by the Syrian government, a military man took him by the hand to a safe house outside Yarmouk, where he paid a further $1,000 to a high-ranking intelligence officer and was driven by a security-force member toward Hama, a city north of Damascus, passing through 30 checkpoints where the officer showed his identity card. In Hama he waited in a basement with many others in the same situation from morning until late afternoon. An Air Force Intelligence officer arrived; they were split into groups of six, put into large cars with reflective glass, and driven to a spot outside the city. Their group was given the name of a high-ranking intelligence officer who would be responsible for making sure they were not arrested, and they waited until dark. Then a large armored car with a big machine gun pulled up, along with two security-agency cars. Women, children and about 20 men climbed into the armored car through the back; he and five other men sat behind the driver's seat, while the driver's colleague sat on ammunition boxes. They traveled for an hour, crossing 19 checkpoints controlled by different government security forces. They were dropped at a large farm in a deserted area and waited another hour while cars came and went. Then three pick-up trucks arrived, driven by Jabhat al-Nusra fighters with the group's flags waving from them. Young people climbed onto the backs of the trucks and were hidden under covers; the rest climbed in behind the driver. They passed through nine checkpoints, handing over money each time. They stopped for one day at a farm near Idlib, then were divided again and driven for five hours in a van with tinted windows to a bus garage under Jabhat al-Nusra's management, where buses could take people to Turkey. The women had to wear the veil, and each woman had to be accompanied by a close adult male relative; some had to pay a further 40,000 Syrian pounds for the trip. They traveled by bus toward a village close to the Turkish province of Hatay. Before the village was a Jabhat al-Nusra checkpoint where some foreign fighters, who hardly spoke Arabic, talked to young people trying to leave Syria about jihad and how it would be a mistake to leave; some of the young men were persuaded and turned back. The last checkpoint before the village was held by Ahrar al-Sham, which had just issued a decision not to take part in smuggling, so some bus drivers had been arrested and many people pushed back. Their driver stopped before the checkpoint and contacted someone he knew; an Ahrar al-Sham van approached and they were transferred into it some distance away, out of sight, then passed through the checkpoint into the village and waited until sunset. They were taken to the top of a hill beside a paved road patrolled by Turkish border guards. The guards arrested them. First they were put in a big tent with nearly 300 men and women, then held on an open-air basketball pitch; it was very cold. At midnight they were given papers in Turkish and told to sign their names, dates of birth and hometowns, promising not to return to Turkey; no one checked what they wrote, so they could write anything. After signing they were taken back to the Syrian border: women and children in buses, the men walking the last kilometer escorted by Turkish guards. The same Ahrar al-Sham driver was waiting on the Syrian side. He drove them back to the same smuggler, and they waited another night, then walked once more toward Turkey on the same route, dozens of them, for nearly an hour, until they crossed the Turkish border, where a large van was waiting. Each of them was forced to pay the smugglers 10,000 Syrian pounds to be taken to the bus station in the Turkish city of Antakya; the smugglers threatened to hand them over to the Turkish security forces if they did not pay. Just before the bus garage they were told to get out and buy bus tickets to Izmir at more than twice the correct price; two men who refused were beaten by the smugglers. From Izmir they went south to the small coastal town of Didim, where smugglers were waiting. They had agreed to pay $700 per person for a boat to Greece. The smugglers made the youths carry the motorized dinghy and engine into the water; about 45 people climbed onto it. Two smugglers boarded and quickly showed one of the passengers how to navigate, then jumped back onto land. They set off from the Turkish coast toward Greece. After more than an hour they neared an island. As they got close, the refugee who was steering suddenly took out a knife and stabbed a hole in the boat; he believed the smugglers had told him to do this so the boat could not be sent back toward Turkey. Everyone fell into the water, including a one-month-old baby, almost drowning. They were helped by travelers who had arrived before them, and, freezing from the water, lit a fire. They discovered they were on an island called Farmakonisi, under the control of the Greek armed forces. They stayed five hours, during which only the children were given a little water and blankets. A boat came and took groups of them to another island, Leros, two hours away. Greek officials took their identity cards and fingerprints and put them in a refugee camp where they were given many relief items; they slept on the pavement inside the camp for lack of space. They got identity papers and were booked onto a 10-hour boat to Athens, for which they paid 41 euros each. From Athens they took a bus to the Macedonian border. A Macedonian military guard tried to send him back to Greece because his identity paper said Palestinian, but they persuaded him that he was Syrian and he was allowed to enter. The Macedonian officials treated them harshly and sometimes even beat women, unlike the Greek military, who had been very kind. They took a train to near the Serbian border, then two buses and a train to Croatia, where police searched them and took photographs and fingerprints. Then they took another train to Slovenia, where police again searched and photographed and fingerprinted them. Then they headed to Austria by train and bus, and finally to the German border. The whole trip from Yarmouk to Germany took 11 days. In Germany he found the country beautiful and the people good, but he felt like a stranger. He was not allowed to work because he lacked the required documents, which added to his loneliness. He felt nostalgia for Syria, even though he is Palestinian by nationality.
